title: Total Parenteral Nutrition
subject: Surgery
summary: TPN delivers all nutrients intravenously when the gut cannot be used. It requires central access, careful monitoring of electrolytes, glucose and lipids, and prevention of line‑related infections.

sections.p: TPN is a complete nutrition solution given through a central venous line when enteral feeding is impossible or contraindicated. Diagnosis is clinical: inability to meet caloric needs orally or enterally for >5–7 days.

Severity is staged by duration and complications: short‑term (≤2 weeks) vs long‑term (>2 weeks). Complications such as catheter sepsis, metabolic derangements or liver dysfunction define advanced stages.
Common causes in low‑resource settings include bowel obstruction, severe pancreatitis, short bowel syndrome, postoperative ileus, and severe infections that preclude oral intake.
Patients appear well‑nourished but have no oral intake, abdominal distension, or signs of ileus. Labs show hyperglycaemia, electrolyte shifts, and rising liver enzymes.
Baseline and ongoing labs guide composition and detect complications.

t.b: Assess sodium, potassium, magnesium, calcium – abnormal levels indicate need for adjustment
Monitor for hyperglycaemia or hypoglycaemia – guides dextrose infusion
Elevated transaminases or bilirubin suggest cholestasis or fatty liver
INR, aPTT to detect vitamin K deficiency or liver dysfunction
If fever or catheter site redness – indicates catheter‑related sepsis

sections.p: Urgent signs include sudden fever, chills, catheter site erythema, worsening abdominal pain, or metabolic acidosis. Complications: catheter sepsis, line thrombosis, hyperglycaemia, refeeding syndrome, liver dysfunction, and lipid emboli.

Treat underlying cause, insert a central line, start a balanced TPN solution (carbohydrate, amino acids, lipids, electrolytes, vitamins). Monitor labs daily, adjust composition, and prevent infection with aseptic technique.

t.b: If catheter sepsis – broad‑spectrum covering gram‑positive and gram‑negative organisms; avoid nephrotoxic agents
If INR >1.5 – to prevent bleeding complications

sections.p: Regular review of nutritional status, line integrity, and metabolic parameters. Early transition to enteral feeding when feasible reduces infection risk.

t.b: Assess tolerance and caloric uptake – indicates readiness to stop TPN

sections.p: Parenteral nutrition (PN) without total calories, or enteral feeding via nasogastric tube. Also confused with refeeding syndrome – a metabolic complication of rapid nutrition restart.
Low serum albumin may be normal in TPN patients due to lack of protein synthesis; normal glucose may mask hyperglycaemia if dextrose is not monitored closely.
b: Albumin low but not indicative of malnutrition
Glucose may appear normal if not checked frequently

faq.q: What is the minimum duration of TPN before considering complications?
faq.a: Complications may arise after 2–3 weeks of continuous TPN, especially catheter sepsis and liver dysfunction.

faq.q: Why are lipids given in a separate infusion?
faq.a: Lipids are concentrated; giving them separately prevents hypertriglyceridaemia and allows better control of caloric intake.

faq.q: Can a patient on TPN develop refeeding syndrome?
faq.a: Yes, especially if they are severely malnourished; monitor electrolytes and give thiamine before starting nutrition.

exam: A 30‑year‑old woman with severe pancreatitis is not tolerating enteral feeds. What is the first step in initiating TPN? — Insert a central venous catheter, start a balanced TPN solution, and monitor electrolytes and glucose.

A patient on TPN develops fever and catheter site erythema. What is the most likely complication and immediate management? — Catheter‑related sepsis; obtain blood cultures, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and consider catheter removal.

A TPN patient shows rising transaminases and bilirubin. What does this indicate and how should you adjust therapy? — Early liver dysfunction; reduce lipid infusion rate and consider adding ursodeoxycholic acid.
A child on TPN has hypophosphatemia and muscle weakness. What syndrome is this and what is the treatment? — Refeeding syndrome; give phosphate supplements and thiamine.
A patient on TPN has hyperglycaemia despite insulin infusion. What adjustment is needed? — Increase insulin dose or reduce dextrose concentration in the TPN solution.
A TPN line is clogged after 4 weeks. What is the most appropriate action? — Flush with heparinised saline, reassess line patency, and consider line change if infection suspected.

A patient on TPN develops sudden abdominal pain and distension. What is the differential and first investigation? — Possible bowel perforation or obstruction; obtain an abdominal X‑ray and start broad‑spectrum antibiotics.
